newsitem.title: USA: U.S. suspends reconnaissance flights in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.S. suspends reconnaissance flights in Zaire.

text.p: The United States on Thursday suspended flights of military reconnaissance planes over Zaire after one of the unarmed aircraft apparently came under anti-aircraft fire on Wednesday, the Pentagon said.
"There are no reconnaissance flights today. We are reassessing the flights in the light of the incidents yesterday," Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters.

Bacon stressed that the four-engine Navy P-3 submarine hunter patrol plane, one of two temporarily based in Entebbe, Uganda, and searching for thousands of displaced Rwandan refugees in Zaire, was not hit in Wednesday's incident. He said he expected the flights to resume and possibly fly higher.
It was not known who directed the fire at the plane, the spokesman said.

The move came as the Pentagon continued to make plans for expected participation in a Canadian-led military relief effort for some 500,000 Rwandan refugees who have returned to Rwanda since last week. But many thousands are believed to be still in Zaire after being displaced from camps.

President Bill Clinton has not made a final decision on U.S. participation in the effort, but the Pentagon said this week it was sending 800 Air Force and other "logistical" personnel to airports in Rwanda, Uganda and Kenya to prepare for a humanitarian airlift operation into Rwanda.
Bacon said on Thursday that 195 of the troops had already arrived at Mombasa in Kenya, 160 at Entebbe in Uganda and 10 in Kigali, Rwanda.

Meanwhile, he said, representatives from about 28 countries which have offered to take part in the Canadian-led operation would meet at a U.S. military facility in Stuttgart, Germany, on Friday to assess the situation in central Africa.
That meeting will be chaired by Canadian Army Lt. Gen. Maurice Baril, who has been designated to lead the U.N.-authorised relief effort.

But Bacon said that it was still not clear how many Rwandan refugees remained in Zaire or what the military effort would entail. The United States on Tuesday put on hold a tentative plan to send up to 1,000 combat troops to Goma in Zaire after refugees swarmed out of camps near Goma and walked home to nearby Rwanda.

Bacon said that 45 U.S. military cargo planes were waiting in Europe to go ahead with any relief operation once authorisation was given. But he also said there were indications that up to 100,000 Rwandan refugees might be making their way northward in Zaire toward Goma and might head back to Rwanda eventually.

As for the reconnaissance flights, Bacon stressed that the P-3 on Wednesday was flying at 19,000 feet (5,791 metres) and was several thousand feet (metres) above what the crew believed were eight air bursts of anti-aircraft shells as it flew south of Goma.
"I would expect the flights to be resumed, but I don't know when," he said, adding that the planes might fly even higher in the future to avoid possible anti-aircraft fire.
